strengths: The paper presents an appealing integration of latent intention inference, flow-based occupancy modeling, and generalized policy improvement for offline pre-training and downstream adaptation.
The empirical study is unusually broad, covering 36 state-based and 4 image-based tasks, eight baseline methods, and multiple robotic locomotion and manipulation domains.
Results are strong on difficult long-horizon manipulation domains, especially Jaco, cube-double, scene, and puzzle tasks, where several baselines make little progress.

Experiments generally use multiple seeds, report variability, provide per-task results, and include ablations of intention representations, policy extraction, convergence behavior, and important hyperparameters.
The appendix gives substantial architectural, optimization, dataset, and hyperparameter detail, and reports manageable hardware/runtime requirements.
weaknesses: The central implicit-GPI objective appears mathematically reversed. Equation 8 minimizes L_mu(Q-Q_hat), with L_mu(x)=|mu-1(x<0)|x^2 and mu>0.5. This penalizes overestimation more heavily and approaches the minimum, rather than the claimed maximum, as mu approaches 1. The theoretical claim in Appendix B.2 therefore does not follow from the stated loss. It is unclear whether the experiments implement the written objective or an unstated sign-corrected version.

The pseudocode contains consequential inconsistencies: Algorithm 1 interpolates with z instead of epsilon and uses s-z rather than s-epsilon, while Algorithm 2 has parameter and return-variable mismatches. Together with the expectile-sign problem, these errors substantially impair reproducibility and confidence in the implemented method.

The theoretical discussion overstates what GPI establishes. Maximizing values of behavior-intention policies guarantees improvement only under appropriate exact-value and policy-coverage assumptions; it does not generally imply convergence to the downstream optimal policy. Approximation, prior/posterior mismatch, offline action support, and reward-model error are not analyzed.

Compute comparisons are not controlled. InFOM generates 16 future states through a 10-step ODE solver for each update, yet adaptation speed is compared primarily by gradient steps. Consequently, the claim of faster policy learning does not establish wall-clock or compute efficiency.

Evidence specifically supporting the inferred-intention mechanism is limited. The representation comparison covers only four tasks, the policy-extraction ablation only two, and there is no direct evaluation of intention recovery, posterior collapse, latent consistency, or coverage when sampling from the prior. This is important because the method trains with posterior intentions but performs GPI using prior samples, sometimes with very weak KL regularization.

The headline aggregate improvements obscure mixed results: InFOM is substantially worse than simpler baselines on several cheetah and cube-single tasks and is not uniformly best on quadruped or visual tasks. Statistical significance tests or aggregate confidence intervals are absent.

The experimental protocol uses very large reward-labeled fine-tuning datasets—500K transitions—and evaluates sample efficiency mainly through optimization steps on only two tasks. Performance versus the amount of reward-labeled data would better substantiate the adaptation and sample-efficiency motivation.

There are reporting inconsistencies, including Jaco returns around 700 despite the appendix stating a maximum return and episode length of 250, as well as differences between some textual domain-count claims. These should be resolved before the numerical conclusions can be fully trusted.

Overall, the empirical results are promising, but the incorrect central loss as written and associated reproducibility ambiguities are too serious for acceptance without clarification and corrected experiments or code-level verification.

strengths: The combination of latent intention inference, flow-based occupancy modeling, and expectile-based policy extraction is relevant and potentially useful for offline RL transfer.
The empirical study is broad, covering 36 state-based and 4 image-based tasks, with several baseline families and multiple random seeds.
The paper reports substantial gains on difficult manipulation domains, especially Jaco, cube-double, scene, and puzzle tasks.
Implementation details, computational requirements, hyperparameters, full per-task results, and several component ablations are provided.
weaknesses: The technical specification contains serious inconsistencies. In Algorithm 1, the flow interpolation uses the latent intention z instead of noise epsilon, and the current-flow target is s-z instead of s-epsilon. Since z can be 512-dimensional while the state has a different dimension, the written algorithm is not executable. It also conflicts with Eq. 7.

The claimed ELBO is mathematically invalid for the hyperparameters actually used. Replacing the unit KL coefficient with lambda preserves a lower bound only when lambda is at least one; nearly all reported lambda values are below one. Thus the paper repeatedly calls an objective an evidence lower bound when it need not lower-bound the likelihood.

The optimality discussion for implicit GPI is overstated. GPI over fixed behavior-conditioned occupancy models can dominate represented base policies under strong exactness assumptions, but it does not generally converge to the globally optimal policy merely because a task-specific intention was captured. Offline coverage, approximation error, and whether each conditional occupancy corresponds to a suitable policy are not addressed.

The closest prior method, TD Flows with GPI, is evaluated only as FB+FOM on four selected tasks rather than across the main benchmark suite. This makes it difficult to determine how much of the reported improvement comes from the new intention model and expectile extraction versus the existing flow-occupancy machinery.

The evaluation protocol introduces substantial selection risk. Several sensitive hyperparameters are tuned by domain, evaluated tuning tasks remain in the reported aggregate, and every visual task is tuned individually. Figure 7 confirms extreme sensitivity to lambda and the behavioral-cloning coefficient, including changes from near-zero to near-perfect success.

There are unresolved reporting contradictions. The appendix states that Jaco has a maximum episode return of 250, while Table 4 reports returns around 700. Sections 5.2 and 5.3 also describe different numbers of ablation tasks than their corresponding figures.

The headline 1.8x and 36% improvements are not defined with a transparent aggregation formula or accompanied by statistical tests. Per-task results are highly heterogeneous, with InFOM substantially worse than simpler baselines on several tasks.

The visual evidence is particularly limited: only four tasks are used, some baselines are omitted, each task receives task-specific tuning, and InFOM does not outperform the best baseline on all of them. This is insufficient support for broad claims about image-based or foundation-scale RL.

Overall, the empirical results are interesting, but the incorrect derivation, impossible pseudocode, incomplete closest-baseline comparison, tuning leakage, and inconsistent reporting prevent confidence in the central claims and reproducibility at a top-tier standard.

strengths: The paper presents an interesting synthesis of variational intention inference, temporal-difference flow occupancy modeling, and expectile-based implicit generalized policy improvement.

The empirical scope is unusually broad: 36 state-based and 4 image-based tasks, eight baseline methods, multiple environment families, and results over 8 seeds for state tasks and 4 seeds for visual tasks.
The strongest results on Jaco, Scene, Puzzle, and several visual tasks suggest that generative occupancy modeling may be particularly useful for sparse-reward, long-horizon settings.

The paper includes component ablations, learning curves, hyperparameter sensitivity studies, per-task results, implementation details, runtime estimates, and an open-source implementation, supporting reproducibility.
The motivation, relationship to successor representations, and overall algorithmic structure are generally clear and relevant to offline RL pre-training.
weaknesses: The claimed ELBO is not valid as written for the hyperparameters actually used. The derivation replaces a negative KL term with -lambda KL while retaining a lower-bound inequality, but most reported lambda values are below 1; for lambda<1, the stated inequality goes in the opposite direction. Thus the optimized beta-VAE-style objective should not be presented as an evidence lower bound without qualification.

The pseudocode materially disagrees with the mathematical method: Algorithm 1 interpolates the target future state with z instead of epsilon and uses s-z as the current-flow target instead of s-epsilon. Algorithm 2 also contains inconsistent parameter notation. These are not superficial notation issues because implementing the pseudocode would produce a different algorithm.

There is a major internal inconsistency in the evaluation: Appendix C.1 states that Jaco episodes and maximum returns are 250, whereas Table 4 reports InFOM returns around 687-747. Since these results drive one of the paper's largest claimed improvements, the return definition or evaluation protocol must be corrected and independently clarified.

The theoretical discussion overstates the guarantees of implicit GPI. An upper expectile only approaches an essential maximum as the expectile tends to 1, while experiments use 0.9-0.99. Moreover, behavioral regularization, approximate occupancy and reward models, offline action support, finite sampling, and prior-sampled latent intentions break the direct connection to exact GPI. The claim of convergence to an optimal downstream policy requires substantially stronger assumptions than merely capturing the task-specific intention.

The experiments do not include the crucial control of training the same InFOM architecture from scratch on the reward-labeled data. Because InFOM continues updating its occupancy model during fine-tuning and uses a substantially different, more computationally expensive learning pipeline, comparisons to other pre-training methods do not isolate the value of pre-training or latent-intention learning.

Several headline claims are stronger than the results. InFOM is not best on several domains, many difficult tasks retain very low absolute success rates, ratios against near-zero baselines can be misleading, and no statistical significance analysis is provided. The text is also inconsistent about succeeding on six of eight versus seven of nine domains.

The intention model is evaluated only indirectly through downstream control. There is no analysis of posterior collapse, latent coverage, correspondence between inferred and actual behaviors, sensitivity to violations of the consecutive-transition consistency assumption, or whether samples from the Gaussian prior remain in-distribution for the learned decoder.

The reward predictor is evaluated on generated future states despite being trained only on logged states. No calibration, model-error, or oracle-reward ablation is provided, leaving open whether policy optimization exploits reward-model extrapolation errors.

Overall, the idea and empirical breadth are promising, but the invalid lower-bound argument, inconsistent algorithm specification, unexplained Jaco score scale, and missing same-method no-pretraining control prevent the work from meeting the technical-soundness and evidentiary standard of a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper proposes a coherent and practically relevant combination of variational intention inference, flow-based occupancy modeling, and expectile-based implicit generalized policy improvement. Conditioning long-horizon occupancy predictions on latent behavior modes is a meaningful extension of prior temporal-difference flow methods.

The evaluation is unusually broad for offline RL: 36 state-based and 4 image-based tasks spanning ExORL and OGBench, generally with eight seeds for state tasks, full per-task results, several strong baselines, and additional experiments using RT-1 data with SimplerEnv evaluation.

The empirical results are compelling on several difficult domains. InFOM produces especially large gains on the sparse-reward Jaco tasks and meaningful improvements on multi-stage OGBench manipulation tasks, while also working from image observations.

The paper includes useful component studies covering intention encoders, policy extraction, behavioral-cloning regularization, dataset size, Monte Carlo sample count, convergence speed, and major hyperparameters. Implementation details and computational requirements are reported extensively.
weaknesses: The interpretation of the learned variable as a persistent user intention is not fully supported. The encoder observes only one next state-action pair, and the t-SNE examples largely distinguish local behavioral phases such as pick versus place or flip versus jump. This may reflect short-term state/action structure rather than trajectory-level intent, and no quantitative intention-recovery metric or controlled ground-truth-intention experiment is provided.

The theoretical discussion of implicit GPI overstates what is established. An expectile approaches an essential supremum only in a limiting regime, while the implemented finite expectiles need not approximate a maximum closely. Moreover, standard GPI guarantees presume accurate value functions for coherent policies; locally inferred latent-conditioned occupancies, learned reward models, finite flow samples, offline action distribution shift, and approximate actor optimization introduce errors that are not analyzed. The claim of convergence to an optimal downstream policy therefore relies on very strong assumptions.

Several headline improvements are driven by domains where most baselines nearly fail, while InFOM is not consistently superior elsewhere—for example, it substantially underperforms ReBRAC or MBPO on multiple cube-single and cheetah tasks. Reporting aggregate medians, normalized scores, confidence intervals for cross-task differences, and statistical tests would make the claimed 1.8x and 36% improvements easier to assess.

Compute is not controlled across methods. InFOM evaluates 16 future samples through a 10-step ODE solver during fine-tuning, yet comparisons primarily equalize gradient steps rather than wall-clock time, FLOPs, or inference cost. This matters for the claimed efficiency and faster-policy-learning conclusions.

The additional robotics evidence is limited: the entire RT-1 dataset is reused for both reward-free pre-training and reward-labeled fine-tuning, evaluation is on one simulated task, only four seeds and a selective subset of baselines are used, and a separately pretrained beta-VAE is required. This does not strongly establish general robotic transfer.

The method is sensitive to domain-specific choices of latent dimension, KL weight, expectile, and behavioral-cloning coefficient. The reported sweeps are broad, and image-task hyperparameters are tuned individually, which weakens evidence that the approach transfers robustly without substantial downstream validation and tuning.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: extracting reusable long-horizon information from heterogeneous, reward-free offline RL data.
Combining variational latent conditioning, flow-based occupancy models, and expectile-based policy extraction is conceptually coherent and potentially useful.
The headline evaluation is broad, covering 36 state-based and 4 image-based tasks, with per-task results and 8 seeds for state experiments and 4 seeds for image experiments.
The appendix provides extensive hyperparameter information, dataset-size studies, and several component ablations.
weaknesses: The central claim that the latent variable represents a persistent user intention is insufficiently supported. The encoder observes only one next state-action pair, and the objective does not enforce consistency between encodings at different points of a trajectory. It can therefore encode local state, action, or trajectory phase rather than intention. The t-SNE plots are qualitative, post hoc, and in fact appear to demonstrate separation of temporal phases such as pick versus place; they do not establish recovery of underlying user intentions.

The implicit-GPI theory is overstated. Expectile regression over occupancy values of behavior-conditioned intentions does not generally converge to the optimal downstream policy. At most, ideal generalized policy improvement can dominate the represented behavior policies; global optimality requires substantially stronger coverage and realizability assumptions than the paper states. Approximation error, reward-model error, finite intention sampling, offline action support, and behavioral regularization are omitted from the argument.

The closest baseline is not evaluated comprehensively. FB+FOM, identified as TD flows with GPI and thus the most direct prior method, is tested on only four selected tasks. The full benchmark instead uses FB+IQL, which changes both the occupancy model and the downstream extraction procedure, preventing attribution of gains to the proposed intention encoder or implicit GPI.

The reported gains are uneven and concentrated in domains where nearly all baselines obtain near-zero performance. InFOM is frequently worse than ReBRAC or MBPO on cheetah and cube-single tasks and is not consistently best on quadruped. Ratio-based summaries such as a 1.8x median improvement can be misleading when denominators are close to zero, while no statistical significance tests or principled cross-domain normalized aggregate are provided.

Important controls are missing: training the full architecture without reward-free pre-training, using shuffled or trajectory-inconsistent intentions, measuring occupancy-model likelihood or calibration, quantifying prior-versus-posterior coverage, and comparing against compute-matched alternatives. Most central ablations use only four hand-selected tasks.

Compute comparisons are not controlled. Each InFOM target uses 16 future samples, each requiring a 10-step ODE solve, whereas baselines are compared mainly by equal gradient-step counts. This substantially weakens claims of efficient adaptation, especially without wall-clock, FLOP, or memory comparisons.

There are serious specification errors in the pseudocode. Algorithm 1 interpolates a future state with z rather than Gaussian noise and uses s-z rather than s-epsilon, which is often dimensionally invalid because latent and state dimensions differ. Algorithm 2 alternates Q_phi and Q_psi and initially gives the ELBO the wrong parameter argument; the preliminary critic objective is also written as an arg max of squared error. These inconsistencies materially harm reproducibility.

The robotics extension is weak evidence for real-world relevance: evaluation occurs in SimplerEnv rather than on a real robot, the same RT-1 data are reused for both pre-training and fine-tuning, a separately trained beta-VAE is introduced, and only a small subset of baselines is considered.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite detailed hyperparameter tables: the supplied manuscript contains no usable code link, the image-space flow implementation is underspecified, and substantial domain-specific tuning is performed on tasks that are subsequently included in the reported evaluation.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and meaningful combination of variational intention inference, temporal-difference flow occupancy modeling, and expectile-based implicit generalized policy improvement. The resulting method addresses an important problem: extracting reusable long-horizon information from heterogeneous, reward-free offline data.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad, covering 36 state-based and 4 image-based tasks from ExORL and OGBench, generally using eight random seeds and reporting full per-task results rather than only aggregate scores.

Comparisons span strong and relevant alternatives, including offline RL, representation learning, model-based pre-training, contrastive occupancy estimation, and successor-feature or skill-based approaches. InFOM is particularly effective on difficult sparse or semi-sparse manipulation tasks.

The paper includes useful component studies covering policy extraction, alternative intention representations, behavioral-cloning regularization, dataset size, sampling budget, convergence speed, and major hyperparameters.

The exposition is generally clear, the method is given in equations and pseudocode, and implementation details, compute requirements, tuning ranges, and domain-level hyperparameters are extensively documented.
weaknesses: The theoretical characterization of implicit GPI is overstated. Greedification over occupancy measures of behavior-policy components guarantees improvement over that policy set under appropriate assumptions, but does not generally imply convergence to the optimal downstream policy merely because a task-specific intention was captured.

There is a conceptual tension in the treatment of intentions. The analysis assumes that the same intention persists across consecutive transitions, which transitively suggests trajectory-level consistency, whereas the visualization interprets changing pick and place phases within one trajectory as distinct inferred intentions. Moreover, encoding an intention from a single state-action pair need not identify the underlying user or task when behaviors overlap.

Evidence that the learned variables recover genuine intentions is mainly qualitative and based on t-SNE plots. Quantitative intention-recovery or controlled identifiability experiments would make this central claim substantially stronger.

Several headline gains are concentrated in domains where most baselines nearly fail, while InFOM is worse than strong baselines on a number of easier tasks. The paper would benefit from statistical tests and aggregate metrics that are less sensitive to near-zero denominators than multiplicative improvement claims.

The additional robotics experiment uses RT-1 data but evaluates only in SimplerEnv, reuses the same dataset for pre-training and fine-tuning, and compares against only three selected baselines. It therefore provides limited evidence of real-world robotic generalization.

The method is computationally and statistically demanding: it uses up to millions of transitions, repeated ODE solves, 16 generated future states per value estimate, and sensitive domain-specific tuning of the latent dimension, KL coefficient, expectile, and behavioral-cloning weight. This limits the strength of the scalability and robustness claims.

The pseudocode contains dimensionally inconsistent apparent errors, such as using the latent variable z where Gaussian state-space noise should appear in Algorithm 1. These should be corrected because they impede faithful reproduction.
